#9569. Egg Donation: Is It Private, or a Secret?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

A woman I was working with recently voiced that her biggest concern about using an egg donor was disclosure. She worried about how certain family members might react. She anticipated judgment, unwanted opinions, and criticism.

She wasn't questioning whether egg donation was right for her. Rather, she was questioning who needed to know and whether that knowledge could come back to hurt her or her family.

Take, for example, a woman who decides not to tell her mother-in-law that she used an egg donor. Perhaps their relationship is difficult. Perhaps she knows her mother-in-law has strong opinions about what makes a family.

Naturally, she may worry that her child will be treated or seen differently. And alongside this may be a concern that her own place as a mother will somehow be questioned.

But she may also feel that she has no choice but to hide the information because she fears how her mother-in-law might react.

And keeping something secret does not automatically mean that someone feels ashamed or that their decision is wrong.

While parents have every right to decide who knows about their fertility treatment, donor conception also involves another person: the child. And the child's relationship with this information is different. For the child, it is part of the story of how they came into the world.

Research supports telling donor-conceived children about their origins early, using age-appropriate language and making it part of their developing understanding of themselves, rather than a “one and done” significant conversation when the child is older (Ilioi et al., 2017; Duff & Goedeke, 2024). There can be something deeply reassuring about growing up with this knowledge, rather than having to make sense of it for the first time later in life.

As the child grows, the conversation also grows. Questions change, new feelings emerge, and things that seemed unimportant at five may take on a different meaning at fifteen.

But what happens when parents tell their child about their conception and then ask them not to tell anyone else?

Parents may have understandable reasons for wanting to keep donor conception within the immediate family. They may want to protect their child from judgment, insensitive comments, or rejection.

But imagine a child who has always known they were conceived through egg donation, yet has been told not to mention it to grandparents or friends.

Perhaps a friend asks why they don't look like their mother. The child may want to explain but hesitate, remembering that their parents don't want anyone to know. In this way they are caught between wanting to talk about themselves and worrying about upsetting their parents.

For example, they might say, “My parents needed help from an egg donor to have me.”

Or equally, “I don't really want to talk about that.”

Both are reasonable responses. The important difference is that the choice belongs to them.

It is OK for parents and children to have different feelings about disclosure. What is important is that parents recognize their own anxieties and try not to pass them on to their child. The child should feel free to develop their own feelings about their origins, without carrying the weight of their parents' worries.

This can be a complex challenge for parents to come to terms with. And it doesn't have to be neatly resolved. It can just be.

Not everyone will understand or approve. Some may have deeply held beliefs about genetics and family relationships. Others may ask intrusive questions or make insensitive comments. You cannot necessarily prevent those reactions, but you can decide how much access those individuals have to your private lives.

Depending on your family and community, it may also be important to prepare your child for the fact that people have different ideas about what makes a family. Not everyone will agree with your views, and they don't have to. This too is part of diversity. There are many different ways to be human.

Duff, M. A., & Goedeke, S. (2024). Parents' disclosure to their donor-conceived children in the last 10 years and factors affecting disclosure: A narrative review. Human Reproduction Update, 30(4), 488–527. doi.org/10.1093/humupd/dmae010

Ilioi, E. C., Blake, L., Jadva, V., Roman, G., & Golombok, S. (2017). The role of age of disclosure of biological origins in the psychological wellbeing of adolescents conceived by reproductive donation: A longitudinal study from age 1 to age 14. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 58(3), 315–324. doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.12667

#9568. How to Have Enough: Wendell Berry on Creativity and Love

“Enough is so vast a sweetness, I suppose it never occurs, only pathetic counterfeits,” Emily Dickinson sighed in one of her love letters to Susan an epoch before Kurt Vonnegut, in a short and lovely poem, distilled happiness to the knowledge that you have enough. It is not an easy knowledge to live with amid the commodified counterfeits of happiness that light up these sunset days of Western civilization, with its mesmerism of maximums and its cult of more, materially and spiritually — capitalism goads us to do more in order to own more while the secular church of self-improvement goads us to be more in order to do more.

Against this backdrop, to take a sabbath is a radical act, an act of countercultural courage and resistance, none more radical than a sabbath taken in nature — that eternal pasture of enoughness, which knew from the outset to create just enough more matter than antimatter for the first small seed of something to bloom into everything; which knows daily to make everything, from the electron to the elephant, take up just as much space and energy as it needs to be exactly what it is; which made every life finite and set a limit even to the speed of light.

To be in nature, without doing, is to be reminded that we are nature, too; that we cannot force the creative force that made us; that we need not keep breaking our own hearts on expectation’s cold hard edge of not-enough.

The poet, farmer, and wise elder Wendell Berry, who once defined wisdom as “the art of minimums,” takes up these immense and intimate questions throughout his wonderful collection This Day (public library) — his series of sabbath poems composed between 1979 and 2013, celebrating the sabbath as a “rich and demanding” idea that “gains in meaning as it is brought out-of-doors and into a place where nature’s principles of self-sustaining wholeness and health are still evident,” a place where “the natural and the supernatural, the heavenly and the earthly, the soul and the body, the wondrous and the ordinary, all appear to occur together in the one fabric of creation.”

In the preface, Berry considers how nature calibrates expectation — even in the creative act itself, where inspiration is not a reach for more but a letting be of what is, a surrender to reality, which is miracle enough:

On Sunday mornings I often attend a church in which I sometimes sat with my grandfather, in which I sometimes sit with my grandchildren, and in which my wife plays the piano. But I am a bad-weather churchgoer. When the weather is good, sometimes when it is only tolerable, I am drawn to the woods on the local hillsides or along the streams… In such places, on the best of these sabbath days, I experience a lovely freedom from expectations — other people’s and also my own. I go free from the tasks and intentions of my workdays, and so my mind becomes hospitable to unintended thoughts: to what I am very willing to call inspiration. The poems come incidentally or they do not come at all. If the Muse leaves me alone, I leave her alone. To be quiet, even wordless, in a good place is a better gift than poetry.

In how it thrives on the freedom from expectation, in how it demands a total surrender and breaks the moment it is demanded of, creativity has a lot in common with love. It may be that nature invented love to teach us the art of enoughness — to learn how to open the heart to another without condition or expectation, to be fully welcomed in another heart in order to learn the hardest axiom of being: that we are, and always were, enough.

Love’s salutary alchemy of enoughness comes alive in the second part of Berry’s eight-part sabbath poem of 1994:

Finally will it not be enough, after much living, after much love, after much dying of those you have loved, to sit on the porch near sundown with your eyes simply open, watching the wind shape the clouds into the shapes of clouds?

Even then you will remember the history of love, shaped in the shapes of flesh, ever-changing as the clouds that pass, the blessed yearning of the body for body, unending light. You will remember, watching the clouds, the future of love.

Couple with John J. Plenty and Fiddler Dan — a lovely vintage illustrated fable about the meaning and measure of enough — then revisit this soulful animated adaptation of Berry’s poem “The Peace of Wild Things” and his prose meditation on the nature of the universe lensed through a sunflower.

#9567. Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?

Reality check: the identity of the couple in The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) by Jan van Eyck is not the only contested element in the painting—the woman’s pregnancy, the event and the actuality of the room are also hotly disputed The National Gallery, London

Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842. A few key facts about the dual portrait, showing a youngish man and his idealised wife, could be gleaned just by looking at the work’s prominent Latin inscription, which translates as “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”. Over the years, just about everything else associated with the painting, from its mysterious room to the obscure occasion, has been open to debate, other than the surname of the man—Arnolfini, connected to an extended family of wealthy merchants from Lucca active in 15th-century Bruges, where Van Eyck had his studio.

Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.

Kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely new one. In the late 1840s, the National Gallery’s future first director Charles Eastlake contended that the artist’s inscription, which he thought could be translated as “Jan van Eyck was this [one]”, meant that the painting was also a dual portrait of the artist and his wife. But in the early 1860s, the British art historian W. H. James Weale interpreted a reference in a 16th-century inventory to a certain “hernoul le fin” in the painting, which he regarded as the French version of the Italian surname Arnolfini. The connection between the couple and that family was thus set in stone, though scholars disagree, often vehemently, about which particular member of the Arnolfini clan is shown.

Kemperdick has revisited the inscription, which is unusually large and conspicuously places the artist’s name next to the male figure’s head. He argues this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man. He has also reconsidered the association between the “hernoul le fin” reference and the surname Arnolfini. Citing the early-modern categorisation of the late-medieval work as not a portrait at all, but rather a lewd genre painting, Kemperdick suggests that “hernoul le fin” is not the correct surname of the sitter, but a subsequent and mocking moniker used by later generations to misidentify the man as a “a deceived cheat”. Kemperdick also suggests that a reference to St Margaret in the bedstead statue near the woman’s head serves to identify her as Van Eyck’s wife.

Kemperdick is the curator of German, Netherlandish and French Paintings before 1600 at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which is noted for its Early Netherlandish holdings and has in its own collection a Van Eyck portrait (around 1435-38) of the very same man who appears in the National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait. The two will be shown together in the London exhibition.

Nicholas Flory, the co-curator of Van Eyck: The Portraits along with Emma Capron, the National Gallery’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting, says that he and Capron find Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative”, citing, among other reasons, that the woman in the Bruges portrait, whom we know to be Margaret based on the inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.

Other leading Van Eyck scholars also have their doubts. The German art historian Till-Holger Borchert—now the director of the Suermondt-Ludwig-Museum in Aachen and the former director of Musea Brugge in Bruges—is familiar with Kemperdick’s theory. “I’m not entirely sure I can concur,” he says. He thinks the early-16th-century inventory reference—associated with the painting’s owner at the time, Margaret of Austria, the governor of the Habsburg Netherlands—is a near iron-clad reference to the Arnolfinis. The Ghent University art historian Maximiliaan Martens, who has been involved in the lengthy restoration of Van Eyck’s Ghent Altarpiece, also “doesn’t see any reason to doubt” that the inventory reference is to the Arnolfinis.

The implications of Kemperdick’s theory are far-reaching. Another Van Eyck portrait at the National Gallery, from 1433, showing a much older man than the figure in the Arnolfini Portrait, is now tentatively identified by the London museum as a self-portrait. This, however, cannot be the case if Kemperdick’s theory is correct.

The exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits will label the Berlin work with its previous and longstanding reference to the Arnolfinis, while the Gemäldegalerie, under Kemperick’s guidance, has recently renamed it Portrait of a Man with a Red Chaperon. And the debate about the couple promises to continue long after the show closes in April.

“I have thought for 30 years about this,” Martens says of the figures in the Arnolfini Portrait. He says he is still not sure if the man is Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (who was apparently not married at the time the painting was made) or his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (whose wife had died before the painting was made).

Other aspects of the dual portrait that scholars continue to debate include whether the heavy-bellied woman is actually pregnant (Kemperdick and Martens think that may be possible, while Flory and Capron think she is just gathering up her heavy skirts), and whether the room itself is a real space or an imagined one (imagined, say Flory and Capron; real, says Martens).

Beyond who made it and when, the Arnolfini Portrait remains a mystery, which is in keeping for an artist whose date and place of birth, among other foundational knowledge, is also speculation. Asked to comment on the enigma associated with the Arnolfini Portrait, Borchert says: “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”

The London museum has a remarkable archive and library, available to all, and a research strategy that includes the opening of a new research centre in 2028

The art historian Matthew Holman makes a personal selection from the finest collection of its type—celebrated for the breadth and depth of the story it tells of Western painting up to 1900

The National Gallery’s exhibition of the 15th-century pioneer will include fresh conservation work, remarkable pairings and a possible revelation tied to a famous work

Structured around the artist's time in Antwerp, Genoa and London, the show at Genoa's Palazzo Ducale offers a gorgeous overview, as well as revealing new research

#9566. Rejected for 10 Years, Then She Made History

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Peggy Whitson, a biochemist, applied for 10 years to become an astronaut. Every time she applied, she was turned down. Who applies for the same job for a decade, I thought? Dr. Whitson made it very clear to me that she would become an astronaut. She realized that there was a divide between what the selection committee was looking for and what she was showing them.

Talent is important, as is grit, resilience and a strong work ethic. That’s a baseline, not a differentiator. The difference between those who succeed despite the setbacks, and sustain that success, might just be how they approach challenges.Whitson focused her energy and talents on closing that delta to prove to the astronaut selection committee that she was worthy of their confidence and would become a great astronaut.

When faced with a challenge, high-performers focus on what they can control. Some circumstances are simply beyond their influence. No one can control the weather or the construction noise outside a building where they’re taking an important exam. What distinguishes high-performers is their ability to double down on the variables within their control while managing their response to those beyond it. How you react to what is beyond your control might separate those who can from those who won’t.

High-performers use setbacks as data points. Each one teaches them something new. They review it with painstaking detail. NBA player Zaza Pachulia played in 1,098 basketball games over his 15-year NBA career. After each game, he told me, he would review the video of the game, not to see what he got right, but rather, what he could improve upon (watch my conversation with Zaza Pachulia). High-performers like Pachulia review the feedback and evidence and look to see how they can improve even a fraction of a percent. Compounded they know that it will have an outsized difference between their output and everyone else’s. Then they take action. In their mind, it’s not a question if they will succeed, rather they focus on how. That’s how high-performers focus on controlling what they can control.

It’s a good thing Whitson didn’t quit on her quest to become an astronaut. Eventually, she was accepted and became the first female commander of the International Space Station (ISS), a role she’s held twice. For years she held the record for spending more days in space than any American astronaut of any gender, and eventually, she was promoted to NASA’s Chief Astronaut.

The next time you are faced with a challenge, examine what needs to happen for you to meet your goal, then look at where you are now. Then figure out how to close that gap. A setback is only a failure if you let it simmer. Take control and plan your next steps.

Gotian, R. (2022). The success factor: Developing the mindset and skillset for peak business performance. Kogan Page.

I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

You know that the price of life is death, that the price of love is loss, and still you watch the golden afternoon light fall on a face you love, knowing that the light will soon fade, knowing that the loving face too will one day fade to indifference or bone, and you love anyway — because life is transient but possible, because love alone bridges the impossible and the eternal.

I think about this and a passage from Louise Erdrich’s 2005 novel The Painted Drum (public library) flits across the sky of my mind:

Life will break you. Nobody can protect you from that, and living alone won’t either, for solitude will also break you with its yearning. You have to love. You have to feel. It is the reason you are here on earth. You are here to risk your heart. You are here to be swallowed up. And when it happens that you are broken, or betrayed, or left, or hurt, or death brushes near, let yourself sit by an apple tree and listen to the apples falling all around you in heaps, wasting their sweetness. Tell yourself that you tasted as many as you could.

This, of course, is what life evolved to be — an aria of affirmation rising like luminous steam from the cold dark silence of an indifferent cosmos that will one day swallow all of it. Every living thing is its singer and its steward — something the poetic paleontologist Loren Eiseley captures with uncommon poignancy in his 1957 essay “The Judgment of the Birds,” found in his altogether magnificent posthumous collection The Star Thrower (public library).

Eiseley recounts resting beneath a tree after a day of trekking through fern and pine needles collecting fossils, dozing off in the warm sunlight, then being suddenly awakened by a great commotion to see “an enormous raven with a red and squirming nestling in his beak” perching on a crooked branch above. He writes:

Into the glade fluttered small birds of half a dozen varieties drawn by the anguished outcries of the tiny parents. No one dared to attack the raven. But they cried there in some instinctive common misery, the bereaved and the unbereaved. The glade filled with their soft rustling and their cries. They fluttered as though to point their wings at the murderer. There was a dim intangible ethic he had violated, that they knew. He was a bird of death. And he, the murderer, the black bird at the heart of life, sat on there, glistening in the common light, formidable, unmoving, unperturbed, untouchable. The sighing died. It was then I saw the judgment. It was the judgment of life against death. I will never see it again so forcefully presented. I will never hear it again in notes so tragically prolonged. For in the midst of protest, they forgot the violence. There, in that clearing, the crystal note of a song sparrow lifted hesitantly in the hush. And finally, after painful fluttering, another took the song, and then another, the song passing from one bird to another, doubtfully at first, as though some evil thing were being slowly forgotten. Till suddenly they took heart and sang from many throats joyously together as birds are known to sing. They sang because life is sweet and sunlight beautiful. They sang under the brooding shadow of the raven. In simple truth they had forgotten the raven, for they were the singers of life, and not of death.

Couple with Hannah Arendt on love and how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, then revisit Loren Eiseley on the warblers and the wonder of being.

#9564. Did Darwin Kill the Meaning of Life?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

When asked in school what the meaning of life could possibly be, my friends and I answered "reproduction," seeing this as the natural conclusion of the truth of evolution. As faulty as this view of me and my friends was, it was based on the view that the evolutionary "purpose" of life is essentially reproduction. This, however, is usually not what is asked when faced with the question of what the meaning of life is, or rather what makes life meaningful. What is asked for, though, is some kind of higher, eternal purpose for humans. This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

The strongest argument for existential nihilism has been provided by the naturalist philosopher Daniel Dennett in Darwin’s Dangerous Idea: Evolution and the Meanings of Life. Evolution as a random and blind mechanism involving nothing beyond reproduction, variation, and differential reproductive success is the fundamental law of biology. Natural selection explains the origin of life and man, without any reference to purpose.

However, and from here existentialists get their name, evolution denies these kinds of essences that have "plagued" philosophy since Plato. Everything is in constant change under the blind and random mechanism of evolution. There is no essence, such as rationality or moral sense, that we could attribute to human nature. When Sartre famously remarked that “existence precedes essence,” he meant that it is left for humans themselves to decide who they are.

To sum up: Evolution destroys all notions of teleology in the biological realm. Sommers and Rosenberg, in their review paper of Dennett with the fitting title “Darwin’s nihilistic idea: evolution and the meaninglessness of life,” phrase the conclusions of the Darwinian argument for existential nihilism in the following way:

Darwinism thus puts the capstone on a process which since Newton’s time has driven teleology to the explanatory side-lines. In short, it has made Darwinians into metaphysical Nihilists denying that there is any meaning or purpose to the universe, its contents and its cosmic history.

The theory of evolution dissolves all purposes in, as Dennett puts it, “Darwin's universal acid”: science, therefore, renders God oblivious and takes away the illusion of purpose from our lives. Dennett even goes so far as to attribute the origin of existentialism to Darwin:

Friedrich Nietzsche saw—through the mists of his contempt for all things English—an even more cosmic message in Darwin: God is dead. If Nietzsche is the father of existentialism, then perhaps Darwin deserves the title of grandfather.

When Nietzsche proclaimed that “God is dead,” we are supposed to view science, if not as the murderer then at least as the tool that was used to kill God. While Nietzsche is often taken as a deterrent to where Darwinian philosophy leads, I argue that Nietzsche’s Darwinism is better associated with his ideas about the death of God than with the Übermensch. Even though Nietzsche is often given as an example of a nihilist, most of his work is directed against the destructive consequences of nihilism, once God has been replaced by science, or more accurately, where science left a hole after getting rid of God.

Especially after the horrors of WW2, it is only reasonable to ask how anyone could continue to believe that there is a God or purpose to our lives. Much of existential thinking boils down to the fact, that there is no God and hence, no one to give the universe purpose and meaning to our lives.

Thomas Nagel offers a thought experiment in which humanity realizes that the human race and our whole planet were created by some creatures to farm and eat human flesh. Clearly, he argues, this doesn’t give us the purpose we ask for when asking for the meaning of life. Would the analogy change if it was God who created us for some purpose rather than a powerful alien race? Camus suggests that this may not work either: “I know that I do not know that meaning and that it is impossible for me just now to know it. What can a meaning outside my condition mean to me? I can understand only in human terms.” Even if God exists and has some purpose for us in mind, we cannot grasp it.

If you enjoyed this short essay, you might enjoy the much longer version, on which it is based, where I go into much more detail: click here.

#9563. How to Cope With Loneliness: 5 Mindfulness Practices to Feel More Connected

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

Feeling lonely isn't a personal failing, and you don't have to transform your social life overnight in order to feel more connected. Try these five gentle mindfulness practices.

I live in a rural area, about four miles from my nearest neighbor. My husband works away on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation, which is fairly common where I live. The community is widely scattered, you need a car to get almost anywhere, and there isn’t a great deal of interaction between neighbors. In fact, I suspect many people don’t even know who lives closest to them.

But I want to make something clear: I’m not generally a lonely person.

Loneliness doesn’t only find people with empty calendars or empty houses. It looks different for everyone.

At school, I was labeled a “loner.” I’ve never had a large circle of friends, preferring instead the company of two or three close ones. Those friendships have lasted through the years and many birthdays. Two of my closest friends live in the UK, and we keep in touch through online chats, time difference and all.

#9562. Atom, Archetype, and the Invention of Synchronicity: How Carl Jung and Wolfgang Pauli Bridged Mind and Matter

“Every true theorist is a kind of tamed metaphysicist,” Einstein wrote as he contemplated the human passion for comprehension in the final years of his life. He may well have been thinking about the great Austrian-Swiss theoretical physicist Wolfgang Pauli (April 25, 1900–December 15, 1958), who first postulated the neutrino and was awarded the Nobel Prize for his discovery of the Pauli exclusion principle — a monumental leap in our understanding of the structure of matter. Decades earlier, 21-year-old Pauli had published a critique of Einstein’s groundbreaking theory of general relativity. It greatly impressed the elder physicist, who wrote in astonishment:

No one studying this mature, grandly conceived work could believe that the author is a man of 21. One wonders what to admire most, the psychological understanding for the development of ideas, the sureness of mathematical deduction, the profound physical insight, the capacity for lucid systematic presentation, the complete treatment of the subject matter, or the sureness of critical appraisal.

Indeed, this uncommon fusion of psychological acumen and scientific rigor only intensified as Pauli grew older. Around the time he wrote the paper that spurred Einstein’s praise, Pauli became enchanted with the work of pioneering psychologist William James. After a three-decade immersion in it, and several years after he won the Nobel Prize in Physics, Pauli met the great psychiatrist Carl Jung (July 26, 1875–June 6, 1961), who in turn was deeply influenced by Einstein’s ideas about space and time.

Jung and Pauli struck an unusual friendship, which lasted a quarter century until Pauli’s death and resulted in the invention of synchronicity — acausally connected events, which the observer experiences as having a meaningful connection on the basis of his or her subjective situation, a meeting point of internal and external reality.

Although rooted in Pauli’s interest in dream analysis, their conversations and correspondence went on to explore fundamental questions regarding the nature of reality through the dual lens of physics and psychology. Each used the tools of his expertise to shift the shoreline between the known and the unknown, and together they found common ground in the analogy between the atom, with its nucleus and orbiting electrons, and the self, with its central conscious ego and its ambient unconscious.

Both men were deeply imprinted by this intellectual cross-pollination. In his posthumously published final work, Jung would write:

We do not know whether what we on the empirical plane regard as physical may not, in the Unknown beyond our experience, be identical with what on this side of the border we distinguish from the physical as psychic. Though we know from experience that psychic processes are related to material ones, we are not in a position to say in what this relationship consists or how it is possible at all. Precisely because the psychic and the physical are mutually dependent it has often been conjectured that they may be identical somewhere beyond our present experience, though this certainly does not justify the arbitrary hypothesis of either materialism or spiritualism.

Pauli’s parallel curiosity about mind and matter is perhaps best articulated in by his friend and collaborator Werner Heisenberg — he of uncertainty principle fame — who would later write:

Behind [Pauli’s] outward display of criticism and skepticism lay concealed a deep philosophical interest even in those dark areas of reality of the human mind which elude the grasp of reason. And while the power of fascination emanating from Pauli’s analyses of physical problems was admittedly due in some measure to the detailed and penetrating clarity of his formulations, the rest was derived from a constant contact with the field of creative processes, for which no rational formulation as yet exists.

In their conceptually daring correspondence, collected in Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters, 1932–1958 (public library), the two delve into these parallels between the physical and psychic dimensions of reality. In one of his early letters, Jung considers the analogy Pauli had proposed between the atomic nucleus and the self. He writes in the autumn of 1935:

Generally speaking, the unconscious is thought of as psychic matter in an individual. However, the self-representation drawn up by the unconscious of its central structure does not accord with this view, for everything points to the fact that the central structure of the collective unconscious cannot be fixed locally but is an ubiquitous existence identical to itself; it must not be seen in spatial terms and consequently, when projected onto space, is to be found everywhere in that space. I even have the feeling that this peculiarity applies to time as well as space… A biological analogy would be the functional structure of a termite colony, possessing only unconscious performing organs, whereas the center, to which all the functions of the parts are related, is invisible and not empirically demonstrable.

The radioactive nucleus is an excellent symbol for the source of energy of the collective unconscious, the ultimate external stratum of which appears an individual consciousness. As a symbol, it indicates that consciousness does not grow out of any activity that is inherent to it; rather, it is constantly being produced by an energy that comes from the depths of the unconscious and has thus been depicted in the form of rays since time immemorial.

The center, or the nucleus, has always been for me a symbol of the totality of the psychic, as the conscious plus the unconscious, the center of which does not coincide with the ego as the center of consciousness, and consequently has always been perceived as being external.

Over the following few years, their correspondence focuses primarily on dream analysis — which both Jung and Pauli saw as a means of illuminating scientific motifs in Pauli’s work — but again and again they return to the symmetry of mind and matter. In a letter to Jung from the summer of 1937, Pauli jeers at the narrow materialism of his own field and calls for an openness to other forms of knowing:

Most modern physics also lends itself to the symbolic representation of psychic processes, even down to the last detail. Of course, nothing is further from the thoughts of modern man than the idea of penetrating the secrets of matter in this way … since it seems to him that, relatively speaking, less research has been done on the soul, and it is less familiar than matter.

The following summer, 38-year-old Pauli writes:

After a careful and critical appraisal of the many experiences and arguments, I have come to accept the existence of deeper spiritual layers that cannot be adequately defined by the conventional concept of time.

In 1947, when Jung decided to found an institute dedicated to this field of research, he asked Pauli — who had received the Nobel Prize a year and a half earlier — to be among its sponsors. The physicist gladly agreed. In a letter to Jung from that December, he noted that the parallels between their interests provide “serious evidence that what is developing is indicative of a close fusion of psychology with the scientific experience of the processes in the material physical world.” He peers into that shared future:

It is probably a long journey, one we are only just setting out on, and it will especially entail, as a modifying factor, constant criticism of the space-time concept.

Space and time were virtually turned by Newton into God’s right hand (oddly enough, the position made vacant when he expelled the Son of God from there), and it needed an extraordinary mental effort to bring time and space back down from these Olympian heights. Going hand in hand with this, apparently, is the criticism of the basic idea of classical natural science, according to which it describes objective facts to such an extent that there is absolutely no link between them and the researcher (objectifiability of the phenomena independently of the way in which they are observed.)

Four decades before the revered physicist John Archibald Wheeler (who coined the term “black hole”) made his influential assertion that “this is a participatory universe [and] observer-participancy gives rise to information,” Pauli plants the seed of a grand question:

Modern microphysics turns the observer once again into a little lord of creation in his microcosm, with the ability (at least partially) of freedom of choice and fundamentally uncontrollable effects on that which is being observed. But if these phenomena are dependent on how (with what experimental system) they are observed, then is it not possible that they are also phenomena (extra corpus) that depend on who observes them (i.e., on the nature of the psyche of the observer)? And if natural science, in pursuit of the ideal of determinism since Newton, has finally arrived at the stage of the fundamental “perhaps” of the statistical character of natural laws … then should there not be enough room for all those oddities that ultimately rob the distinction between “physics” and “psyche” of all its meaning…?

If you turn Pauli’s words over in your mind for a few moments, you’d realize just how radical and enormous a proposition this is. Indeed, it was this letter that catalyzed the series of conversations in which Pauli and Jung came up with the concept of synchronicity — the ultimate dependency between the observer and the observed. By the fall of 1948, they were using the term regularly in their correspondence. In a letter from mid-1949, Jung writes to Pauli, enclosing a manuscript of his first paper on the subject:

Quite a while ago, you encouraged me to write down my thoughts on synchronicity… Nowadays, physicists are the only people who are paying serious attention to such ideas.

A few days later, Pauli echoes this faith in interdisciplinary thinking by sharing with Jung one of his great intellectual influences:

The idea of meaningful coincidence — i.e., simultaneous events not causally connected — was expressed very clearly by Schopenhauer in his essay “On the Apparent Design in the Fate of the Individual.”

This essay of Schopenhauer’s had a lasting and fascinating effect on me and seemed to be pointing the way to a new trend in natural sciences. But whereas [he] wanted at all costs to cling to the rigid determinism along the lines of the classical physics of his day, we have now acknowledged that in the nuclear world, physical events cannot be followed in causal chains through time and space. Thus, the readiness to adopt the idea on which your work is based, that of the “meaning as an ordering factor,” is probably considerably greater among physicists than it was in Schopenhauer’s day.

In a subsequent letter from the autumn of 1950, Pauli — who preferred the term “meaning-correspondence” over “synchronicity” as a way of placing greater emphasis on the meaning of events than on their simultaneity — adds:

In truth, nature is so fashioned that — analogous to Bohr’s “Complementarity” in physics — any contradiction between causality and synchronically can never be ascertained…. How do the facts that make up modern quantum physics relate to those other phenomena explained by you with the aid of the new principle of synchronicity? First of all, what is certain is that both types of phenomenon go beyond the framework of “classical” determinism.

I nevertheless, as a physicist, have the impression that the “statistical correspondence” of quantum physics, seen from the point of view of synchronicity, is a very weak generalization of the old causality… Although microphysics allows for an acausal form of observation, it actually has no use for the concept of “meaning.”

In the letter, Pauli diagrams the concepts discussed:

Six days later, Jung picks up the thread and crystallizes the definition of synchronicity:

Synchronicity could be understood as an ordering system by means of which “similar” things coincide, without there being any apparent cause.

With an eye to Pauli’s diagram, he considers the role of space and time in synchronicity:

Modern physics, having advanced into another world beyond conceivability, cannot dispense with the concept of a space-time continuum. Insofar as psychology penetrates into the unconscious, it probably has no alternative but to acknowledge the “indistinctness” or the impossibility of distinguishing between time and space, as well as their psychic relativity. The world of classical physics has not ceased to exist, and by the same token, the world of consciousness has not lost its validity against the unconscious… “Causality” is a psychologem (and originally a magic virtus) that formulates the connection between events and illustrates them as cause and effect. Another (incommensurable) approach that does the same thing in a different way is synchronicity. Both are identical in the higher sense of the term “connection” or “attachment.” But on the empirical and practical level (i.e., in the real world), they are incommensurable and antithetical, like space and time.

I would now like to propose that instead of “causality” we have “(relatively) constant connection through effect,” and instead of synchronicity we have (relatively) constant connection through contingency, equivalence, or “meaning.”

He illustrates this proposition with his own variation on Pauli’s diagram:

In a letter sent twelve days later, Pauli responds by introducing the crucial concept of scale into these considerations of synchronicity:

Synchronicity should be defined in a narrower sense so as to comprise effects that only appear when there is a small number of individual cases but disappear when there is a larger number… In quantum physics, there are not just effects that appear with large numbers instead of with small ones, and not only is the term “meaning” not the right one here (which you have written about at great length) but also the concept of the (psychic or psychoid) archetype cannot be used so lightly in the acausalities of microphysics.

In a letter from October of 1953, more than twenty years into their correspondence and a decade into their shared obsession with synchronicity, Jung writes to Pauli:

It means a lot to me to see how our points of view are getting closer, for if you feel isolated from your contemporaries when grappling with the unconscious, it is also the same with me, in fact more so, since I am actually standing in the isolated area, striving somehow to bridge the gap that separates me from the others. After all, it is no pleasure for me always to be regarded as esoteric. Oddly enough, the problem is still the same 2,000-year-old one: How does one get from Three to Four?

Jung and Pauli unfurl many more fascinating parallels between psychology and physics in the remainder of Atom and Archetype. Complement it with Jung on human nature, then revisit physicist, novelist, and poet Alan Lightman on science and transcendence.

#9561. The Most Dangerous Compliment You Can Receive

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

We have probably all met someone along the way who impressed and attracted us with their charm, charisma, and positive attention. Yet at times, they may have made us feel unsettled with their praise. Their flattery may have been enjoyable at the beginning, but over time, some of the compliments may have gone over the top and made us uncomfortable. From our “stunning” appearance to our “brilliant” intellect, the acclaim was unmerited and even arguably untrue. What is their motivation? Research investigates this question.

In the course of my almost 30 years as a prosecutor, I have observed one of the most seductive techniques used by sexual predators and human traffickers to be targeting young women who are not used to receiving positive attention. Having grown up in the shadow of much prettier peers and classmates, they are uniquely vulnerable to the unmerited compliments and advances of handsome (usually much older) men. Yet this dynamic is not limited to criminal perpetrators; it is used in everyday life by people seeking to manipulate and exploit people and resources.

Benjamin A. Rogers et al. (2023) discussed the impact of praise in a study entitled, “Too Naïve to Lead: When Leaders Fall for Flattery.”[1] They identify flattery as one of the “oldest and most commonly used” tactics of impression management, one that frequently benefits the flatterer. Yet flattery also impacts the recipient, who may reward the praise, inadvertently compromising their perception. Managers are apparently not immune from this dynamic, as Rogers et al. note that when they reward flatterers, they risk being viewed as naïve. And “falling for flattery” can compromise impressions of both leaders and the organizations they represent.

Yet if you know what to look for, you can detect it.

As a practical matter, false compliments often target idealized traits you would love to have but know you do not. A false flatterer will comment on your gorgeous figure or uncanny knack for solving complex problems—with very little or no evidence to support their compliments. In such instances, motivation is inherently suspect. “What do you want?” you might ask jokingly, when, actually, that is a very good question. Because many compliments are paired with an “ask,” requesting us to do something for the praise-giver, which puts their motivation under greater scrutiny. This is especially suspect when your denial of the request is met with hostility or expressions of disappointment.

The more challenging example is when you receive compliments in borderline areas where you may indeed possess some degree of the appearance or aptitude alleged. Here, we wonder whether our vocal admirer is merely viewing us with positive bias through rose-colored glasses. Yet if that is the case, they are unlikely to include a request, and certainly not become hostile or rude when we refuse.

Another red flag is mixing praise with criticism. This method of manipulation is designed to make us unsteady and anxious, leading some people to feel the need to behave in a certain way in order to be rewarded with flattery, instead of disheartened by criticism.

So, whether you are the boss or a new employee, a friend or potential paramour, keep your emotional antenna up both professionally and personally, and receive praise responsibly.

[1] Rogers, Benjamin A., Ovul Sezer, and Nadav Klein. “Too Naïve to Lead: When Leaders Fall for Flattery.” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 125, no. 6 (2023): 1394–1419.

#9560. Show of every Jan van Eyck portrait reveals many new sides to his works

Jan van Eyck’s Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439) is one of nine panel portraits the artist made that still survive, and all have been brought together in the National Gallery show Photo: National Gallery London; © Musea Brugge

There is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born. What we do know is that his career—from the early 1420s until his death in 1441—helped launch the Early Netherlandish school, influencing the use of oil paint far beyond his native Low Countries and instilling a new and arguably everlasting value of verisimilitude in Western art.

But we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait. The bijoux blockbuster show will give scholars a unique opportunity to compare scattered works of singular importance. Van Eyck: The Portraits—with a checklist that expands all the way to 13 through the addition of three works on paper by his followers—is built around some remarkable pairings.

Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

The National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Van Eyck’s enigmatic view of an elegantly dressed couple in an impressive reception room, will be shown for the first time with its related work from the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin clearly showing the same man, Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) (around 1435-38).

Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is loaning Portrait of an Elderly Man (A Scholar?) (around 1438). It will be shown with the preparatory drawing from Dresden, in goldpoint and silverpoint on prepared paper, with its revealing notes on how to colour the painting itself.

Van Eyck’s devotional portraits, such as those in his groundbreaking Ghent Altarpiece and the Musée du Louvre’s recently treated Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (around 1435), are outside the scope of the National Gallery exhibition.

Some of the portraits have reverse imagery of fictive marble, and the museum is placing them in cases so visitors can view both sides. “We’re really excited to be able to show people how amazing the reverse is,” says Nicholas Flory, who is curating the show along with Emma Capron, the museum’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting. Flory says the elaborate reverses suggest that “these objects were not designed for a single kind of specific space or to be flat against the wall”, but rather “to be interacted with”.

Newness abounds in the show. The Arnolfini Portrait had long had an ornate Gothic Revival frame until it was replaced in 2024 by a 15th-century gilded frame. Meanwhile, the Berlin work, showing its male figure in distinctive red chaperon headgear, completed a conservation treatment in 2023 that removed distorting yellow varnish. The result of that treatment, says Stephan Kemperdick, the curator of Netherlandish paintings before 1600 at the Gemäldegalerie, has been to “make the palette cooler”. Before, he says, the chaperon was “fire-engine red”, and the man’s face looked “suntanned”, whereas now, he says, the face is “pinkish or whiteish—a feature that distinguished people from the better classes in the 15th century”.

The London exhibition, which Kemperdick calls a “once-in-a-lifetime” event, is a culmination of sorts. Several Van Eyck works, including the Ghent Altarpiece, have undergone recent treatments, which Flory says has been “an impetus in Van Eyck scholarship”, and the National Gallery show reflects new research into Van Eyck’s technique, his original frames and inscriptions. Recent analysis of the National Gallery’s self-portrait, examined during its recent treatment, revealed how Van Eyck modulated the blueness of the background in the lower-right corner to “throw the sitter’s shoulder forward”, Flory says, creating a 3D effect.

Just out of view of the show itself, lurking in Kemperdick’s catalogue essay, is a possible bombshell: that the couple shown in the Arnolfini Portrait are not the titular Italian merchant and his wife at all, but rather Van Eyck and his wife. This would also mean that the Gemäldegalerie’s Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) is also a self-portrait.

The Arnolfini Portrait is among the gallery’s most popular works, and the minuscule size of the show is in marked contrast with the likely museumgoer interest. However, Flory says the diminutive roster is, in fact, the big attraction.

“There was the possibility to expand it beyond Van Eyck and show his work in the context of his contemporaries,” Flory says. “But because he is such a monumental figure in the history of Western painting, and his portraits are so special, we really wanted to focus the exhibition on just Van Eyck himself.” Luckily, he adds, the remarkable loans, which have involved several museums sending some of their most precious works, mean “we got everything we were hoping for”.

• Jan van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

The FI community has identified several strategies that can significantly reduce the tax bite on Social Security benefits. The key insight: since taxation is based on combined income, controlling your income in retirement is the lever.

This is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

The math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

For single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

No. Social Security benefits are not earned income. They are classified as unearned income for tax purposes. This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

No — and this is why Roth accounts are so powerful in retirement. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula used to determine Social Security taxation. Converting Traditional IRA money to Roth before claiming Social Security can dramatically reduce the tax on your benefits for life.

Yes. File Form W-4V with the Social Security Administration to have federal income tax withheld from your benefits. You can choose 7%, 10%, 12%, or 22% withholding. This avoids the surprise of a large tax bill at filing time. State tax withholding varies by state.

Social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

Yes, Social Security benefits can be taxable — up to 85% of your benefits may be added to your taxable income depending on your combined income. The thresholds are low ($25,000 single, $32,000 married) and haven't been adjusted for inflation since 1993, catching more retirees every year. The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Every dollar in a Roth account is a dollar that won't push your Social Security into the taxable zone. Plan your retirement income sources deliberately, and you can reduce or eliminate this tax entirely.

#9558. AI Can Simulate Empathy, but It Can’t Replace Psychotherapy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

A few months ago, NPR ran the story, “She told no one about her agony except ChatGPT. What her death reveals about AI risks.”1 What’s heartbreaking about the article is that the woman who died by suicide, Sophie Rottenberg, had a human psychotherapist, and yet her use of the AI therapist was so engrossing that she didn’t share her suicidal feelings with her living, human psychotherapist.

Sadly, Rottenberg is not an anomaly and instead points to something occurring far too regularly. In my last blog, I introduced the concept of the cultural unconscious to describe an underlying dimension of psychological life shaped by our shared cultural experiences. It encompasses collective images, practices, beliefs, and conflicts that circulate within a culture without complete conscious awareness.

The cultural unconscious shapes how we perceive ourselves and others, interpret our experiences, and engage with the world. One dominant cultural experience expressed in the cultural unconscious is what Dr. Sherry Turkle, MIT professor of the social studies of science and technology and a clinical psychologist, calls a “flight from conversation.” She argues in her book Reclaiming Conversation: The Power of Talk in a Digital Age that our constant tether to smartphones and digital devices has triggered it.2

We communicate more through texts, emails, and social media, but we connect less. We aren’t having as many spontaneous, face-to-face, and depthful conversations in real time. Instead, we’re inundated with numerous, remote, superficial messages that interrupt our attention—texts, tweets, alerts, snaps, emails—which are disconnected from organic, human dialogue.2 It is nearly inescapable in our culture. Turkle cites research showing that the mere presence of a phone—even a silent phone on a table—alters the quality of a conversation, keeps topics more superficial, and lowers empathy.

As chatbots become more embedded in our culture, people are naturally turning to them for connection and mental health support. Conversation requires work, sustained attention, and engagement. It can be hard to be vulnerable with someone in real time, which often brings fear of judgment. Chatbots are a ready-made solution: instantly available, inexpensive, highly responsive, and offering responses that frequently align with what we hope to hear.

With the ease and accessibility of ChatGPT and Claude, more people are confessing what they may be too scared, ashamed, or psychologically defended to say out loud to another human being, even a psychotherapist. This fear and shame are magnified by critical public discourse that pushes this behavior underground, which can become even more dangerous when concealed. Secretive AI chatting feeds tragic situations we keep reading about—people committing suicide, not taking their medications, believing delusions, and more.

Again, part of AI’s allure is that it’s nonjudgmental and affirming, proclaiming, “Great idea,” and “You’re so right.” Such responses can be seductive both to people who feel inferior and/or superior. AI can bolster those who feel inferior while affirming those who feel superior, a dynamic that resonates with a 2026 study linking higher narcissism, individualism, and intolerance of uncertainty to more problematic AI use.3 For someone struggling with self-worth (i.e., narcissism), the assurance of being met with acceptance and praise can be intoxicating. So, too, is the illusion of empathy that AI provides. Genuine empathy is not synonymous with agreement or approval. Yet the human mind can conflate feeling understood with being validated, mistaking empathic understanding for affirmation of beliefs and behaviors.

If a person is struggling, they often want empathy reflected back, and many humans cannot consistently communicate that way. AI has been trained to produce the language of empathy, which many people lack in their relationships. However, AI cannot offer the relational and psychological processes that make empathy transformative, as it does in psychotherapy.

Initially, when AI responds with “That sounds so hard,” it may sound like music to one’s ears, especially when someone gets dismissive comments like “Sorry to hear that” from others in their life. When someone longs for care and understanding, a machine that says exactly what we want to hear can be comforting for a time. However, these affirming responses can only go so far, particularly when someone is suffering psychologically.

The psychological tools, education, and support that AI provides should not be confused with genuine psychotherapy. Despite having no professional qualifications, Rottenberg’s chatbot was touted as a highly knowledgeable therapist and introduced itself as “I am Harry, your personal therapist, and I’m here to support you.” As an AI chatbot, Harry simulated the language, empathy, and authority of a psychotherapist, but lacked the clinical judgment, relational responsibility, and ethical accountability required of licensed psychotherapists. Harry encouraged Rottenberg to seek help, create a safety plan, and confide in loved ones, but as a chatbot, it could not call her parents, alert authorities, or escalate the situation. Nor could it offer the relational, nuanced experience that human connection provides.

A common misconception is that psychotherapy primarily provides emotional support, a place to vent, problem-solving, advice, tools, or answers. Some people only experience this, reinforcing the belief that this is what psychotherapy primarily offers. In part, this is happening more frequently as therapy sessions are limited, psychotherapist training programs fail to educate comprehensively, and clinicians are overworked and undercompensated. As I’ve written about the limits of diagnosis, “being in treatment” involves knowing and being known. It’s being followed longitudinally and is not merely a place to vent or receive advice. Lasting psychological change requires more than these interventions.

Research highlights the importance of the therapeutic relationship and distinct therapeutic processes that support longer-term, meaningful change, including engaging with emotional experience, fostering insight, strengthening relational capacities, and helping individuals recognize and transform entrenched patterns.

Unlike chatting with AI, a skilled, ethical, and effective psychotherapist won’t offer complete understanding, affirmation, and unequivocal support. Rather, real psychotherapy includes relational conflict, pushback, discomfort, and difficult or negative emotions. Working through these challenges is central to psychotherapy. It’s a fluid, dynamic, and emergent process that unfolds between psychotherapist and patient, with each bringing their own reactions, emotions, and thoughts into the therapeutic container.

Chatting with AI comes with real issues and risks, yet AI can offer psychological education and support. It’s important to remember it cannot provide psychotherapy, although it can be a helpful adjunct. In my next post, I’ll explore issues related to AI and psychotherapy, including a case study in which AI enhanced the therapeutic process.

1. Chatterjee, R. (2026, Aug. 18). She told no one about her agony except ChatGPT. What her death reveals about AI risks. NPR. https://www.npr.org/2026/08/18/nx-s1-5929575/ai-suicide-risks-mental-health

2. Turkle, S. (2015). Reclaiming conversation: The power of talk in a digital age. Penguin Press.

3. Kırcaburun, K. (2026). Dark tetrad traits and problematic generative artificial intelligence use: The serial mediating role of individualism and intolerance of uncertainty. BMC Psychology, 14(1), 1220. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05012-4

#9557. Elisha Goldstein: A Nourishing Breath Meditation

The most trusted resource for mindfulness and meditation.

The deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are. This simple awareness of breath practice is an act of self-love and compassion for the moment we find ourselves in.

Mindful breathing often serves as the foundation for meditation practices because your breath is always with you, wherever you are, and it can be used as an anchor to the present moment. In essence, all that’s involved is simply being mindful when you breathe in and out. There is no need to analyze, count, visu­alize, or manipulate the breath in any way. Just breathe normally and naturally and be aware of breathing in and out. There are a few methods you can use to focus on your breath. You can be mindful of your breath in your nose, chest, belly, or even your entire body as it breathes in and out.

With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are.

For dealing with the challenges of stress and anxiety, we sometimes recommend abdominal breath­ing—breathing from the belly, rather than only into the chest—as this can be very calming. However, if another location is preferable, please listen to your own wisdom. Generally speaking, abdominal or belly breathing is the way we all naturally breathe, especially when we’re lying down. To determine if you’re breathing from your abdomen, place your hand on your belly and feel whether it expands as you inhale and contracts as you exhale. If it doesn’t, turn your attention to breathing more deeply and feeling your belly expand and contract with your breath.

An important benefit of abdominal or belly breathing is that it helps moderate irregular breathing patterns, which often arise due to stress or irritation. Anxiety can lead to shallow, rapid, or sporadic breathing and even hyperventilation, and a full-blown panic attack can cause increased shortness of breath, thoughts of losing control, and pains in the chest. By bringing the breath back into the belly, you can help the body return to balance. So when anxiety arises, first acknowledge the feeling, then gently bring attention to the abdomen and practice mindful belly breathing.

Before we begin, we have one final bit of advice: With any of these practices, the deepest healing occurs when you come to terms with the way things are. This might mean simply noticing and acknowledging stress or anxiety rather than falling into old patterns of running away from it. You may discover that by embracing your fear you find your heart.

Do this practice in a relaxing environment without distractions, such as the phone. You can do it either lying down or sitting up, but if you lie down and find yourself falling asleep, try a more upright posture. Bring your full, undivided attention to this practice as you listen or read the following meditation, pausing after each paragraph. You can practice anytime throughout the day, combining this practice with the mindful check-in if you like.

Read and practice the guided meditation script below, pausing after each paragraph. Or listen to the audio practice.

This practice excerpted from A Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Workbook, by Bob Stahl and Elisha Goldstein. New Harbinger Publications
